twins.question: In Java, what does s1 == s2 compare when s1 and s2 are String objects?
options: Whether their characters are the same
Whether both variables refer to the same object
twins.explanation: For objects, == compares references: it is true only when both variables point to the very same object. To compare the characters, use s1.equals(s2).
hints: For objects, does == look inside them, or at where they live?
Which method would you call if you wanted to compare the characters instead?

twins.explanation: a.equals(b) compares characters, so it is true. Each new String(...) creates a separate object, so a != b is also true. true && true prints true.
hints: Work out a.equals(b) first. What does equals compare?
Now a != b: did 'new' create one object or two?

twins.explanation: For overridden methods Java picks the version from the actual object's class at run time (dynamic dispatch). The object is a Dog, so Dog's speak() runs, even though the variable's type is Animal.
hints: What type is the variable, and what type is the object it points to?
For an overridden method, which of those two does Java look at when the program runs?

twins.explanation: obj has type A but refers to a B object. show() is overridden in B, and Java chooses the overriding method from the real object at run time, so it prints B.
hints: Which class's object was actually created with new?
When a method is overridden, does Java use the variable's type or the object's type at run time?

twins.question: A static field in a Java class is…
options: Shared by all objects of that class
Recreated every time a method is called
twins.explanation: A static field belongs to the class itself, not to any one object. There is a single copy, and every object of the class reads and writes that same copy.
hints: Does a static field belong to the class or to each object?
If there is only one copy, who shares it?

twins.explanation: n is static, so all objects share one copy. Each constructor call adds 1 to that same copy: three objects make n equal 3.
hints: How many copies of n exist: one per object, or one in total?
Each constructor adds one to n. How many constructors ran?
